note: Orders every 3 days, both goods together, about 15% safety stock; the main risk is the cash squeeze on day 6 just before the day-10 spike, which can leave goods short.
Orders every 2 days with 10% safety stock: low holding cost and easy on cash; the risk is a higher fixed cost (13×47) and shortages from a thin buffer.
Large batches every 4 days to save on the fixed fee; the risk is overflowing the 152-unit capacity and running out of cash early, which means big shortages around day 10.
Lean 3-day cycle ordering exactly the forecast with no safety stock; the risk is systematic shortage, since the multiplier averages 1.046 and a shortage costs 12 vs about 1 for leftovers on good 0.
3-day cycle with a heavy 30% buffer; the risk is that cash cuts the orders early on and later arrivals overflow capacity and get lost.
Good 0 every 2 days, good 1 every 4 days in larger batches (it has shorter shelf life but is cheap); the risk is the fixed cost, same as in the 2-day plan, plus spoilage of good 1.
Shifted 3-day cycle (days 0, 2, 5, 8, …, 23) so the batches line up better with the spike and the end of the horizon; the risk is too little cash on day 5 to cover the day-10 spike.

Orders every 2 days with a larger buffer on good 0 (about 25%, since a shortage costs 12 and a leftover only 0.4 per day); the risk is cash truncating the day-6 order and paying the fixed fee 13 times.
